(CNN) -- Remember the worst job you ever had? You know, back when there were jobs to be had? Jesse Eisenberg tries to strike up a relationship with Kristen Stewart in "Adventureland." For writer-director Greg Mottola, it was the summer he spent on hiatus between college and the real world, working as a carny at the local carnival. He's turned the experience into the basis for the wonderful "Adventureland." Handing out stuffed animals to the lucky customer whose tin horse romps home in first place -- this is not how James (Jesse Eisenberg from "The Squid and the Whale") would choose to see himself. The paycheck is dismal, but undeniably commensurate with (as a character puts it) "the work of pathetic, lazy morons," which is what it comes down to. Most jobs have their compensations, though. At Adventureland, for James, the biggest benefit comes in the form of Em (Kristen Stewart), another recent grad with plans to move to New York in the fall, and who isn't entirely disdainful of his company. Last time out of the gate Mottola enjoyed a hit with the spectacularly lewd "Superbad," an angle that Miramax Films is understandably keen to play up in the marketing this time around. At first glance the cap seems to fit. James' sexual experience -- or rather the lack of it -- is a defining element in the story. "Adventureland" comes with the usual farcical peccadilloes of teen comedy -- barf gags, car wrecks and inopportune erections -- as well as several familiar supporting players from the Judd Apatow stable. Bill Hader and Kristen Wiig are engagingly upbeat as the mutually besotted park managers, and Martin Starr (from "Freaks and Geeks") is James' cerebral, pipe-smoking buddy, Joel. (Mottola directed a couple of episodes of Apatow's short-lived Fox series "Undeclared.") There's also an extended cameo from Ryan Reynolds, an actor whose faintly supercilious good looks have graced innumerable dumb slacker comedies, including "Van Wilder," "Harold & Kumar Go to White Castle" and "Waiting." Yet, after an initial flurry of gross guffaws, the movie edges toward something rather different: a nuanced, sensitive coming-of-age story that finds its heart in post-adolescent romantic turmoil. Obviously adept with actors, Mottola respects his characters too much to let first impressions stick. The relationships in "Adventureland" are much richer, and stickier, for it. The understanding that James arrives at with his father (Jack Gilpin), for example, is delineated in just a handful of looks and glances between them, but it's enough to imply the older man's resignation at his fate, and his appreciation for James' tacit sympathy. It's in moments like these (and there are a number of them) that we're reminded Mottola made a fine indie movie, "The Daytrippers," more than a decade ago now, another sharp and tender comic distillation of family bonds and fractures. Blessed with comical seriousness, Eisenberg is like a young Woody Allen: fretful, intelligent, naive and deluded. And like Allen, he seems to enjoy more than his fair share of luck with the opposite sex. Still, "Adventureland" makes more effort than "Superbad" -- not that hard admittedly -- to develop a character for Stewart. Looking wan and pensive (the "Twilight" star always looks in need of a good night's sleep), Stewart as Em gives the impression she's living life more acutely than the others. She seems to have more on the line. Set in the mid-'80s, the film suggests the period unobtrusively, but predominantly through pop music. Lou Reed provides sweet relief to repeated bursts of Falco's "Rock Me Amadeus." Yes, in retrospect, that's exactly what being young in 1987 was like. A mature movie about immature young people, "Adventureland" may be too muted to succeed in today's marketplace, too sensitive for its own good. Like an anxious parent, a critic can only send it on its way and hope the world treats it well. "Adventureland" is rated R and runs 107 minutes. For Entertainment Weekly's take, click here.

(CNN) — Remember the worst job you ever had? You know, back when there were jobs to be had?

Jesse Eisenberg tries to strike up a relationship with Kristen Stewart in *Adventureland*. For writer-director Greg Mottola, the inspiration was the summer he spent in limbo between college and the real world, working as a carny at a local amusement park. He has transformed that experience into the foundation for the wonderful *Adventureland*.

Handing out stuffed animals to the lucky customer whose tin horse romps home in first place is not how James (Jesse Eisenberg of *The Squid and the Whale*) would choose to see himself. The paycheck is dismal, but undeniably commensurate with, as one character puts it, “the work of pathetic, lazy morons,” which is what the job ultimately amounts to.

Most jobs, however, have their compensations. At Adventureland, for James, the greatest benefit arrives in the form of Em (Kristen Stewart), another recent graduate with plans to move to New York in the fall—and someone not entirely disdainful of his company.

Mottola’s previous film was the spectacularly lewd hit *Superbad*, an association Miramax Films is understandably eager to emphasize in its marketing this time around. At first glance, the label seems to fit. James’s sexual experience—or, more precisely, the lack of it—is a defining element of the story. *Adventureland* includes the customary farcical peccadilloes of teen comedy: barf gags, car wrecks, and inopportune erections, along with several familiar supporting players from the Judd Apatow stable.

Bill Hader and Kristen Wiig are engagingly upbeat as the mutually besotted park managers, while Martin Starr of *Freaks and Geeks* plays James’s cerebral, pipe-smoking friend, Joel. Mottola also directed a couple of episodes of Apatow’s short-lived Fox series *Undeclared*. There is also an extended cameo from Ryan Reynolds, an actor whose faintly supercilious good looks have graced innumerable dumb slacker comedies, including *Van Wilder*, *Harold & Kumar Go to White Castle*, and *Waiting*.

Yet after an initial flurry of gross-out laughs, the film edges toward something rather different: a nuanced, sensitive coming-of-age story that finds its emotional center in post-adolescent romantic turmoil. Clearly adept with actors, Mottola respects his characters too much to allow first impressions to harden into caricature. The relationships in *Adventureland* are richer—and more complicated—for it.

The understanding James reaches with his father (Jack Gilpin), for example, is conveyed in just a handful of looks and glances between them, yet it is enough to suggest the older man’s resignation to his fate, as well as his appreciation for James’s tacit sympathy. It is in moments like these—and there are several—that we are reminded Mottola made the fine indie film *The Daytrippers* more than a decade ago, another sharp and tender comic distillation of family bonds and fractures.

Blessed with a kind of comical seriousness, Eisenberg recalls a young Woody Allen: fretful, intelligent, naïve, and deluded. And, like Allen, he seems to enjoy more than his fair share of luck with the opposite sex.

Still, *Adventureland* makes more effort than *Superbad*—admittedly not a high bar—to develop Stewart’s character. Looking wan and pensive—the *Twilight* star always appears in need of a good night’s sleep—Stewart, as Em, gives the impression of someone living life more acutely than those around her. She seems to have more at stake.

Set in the mid-1980s, the film evokes the period unobtrusively, though predominantly through pop music. Lou Reed provides sweet relief from repeated bursts of Falco’s “Rock Me Amadeus.” Yes, in retrospect, that is exactly what being young in 1987 felt like.

A mature film about immature young people, *Adventureland* may be too muted to thrive in today’s marketplace, too sensitive for its own good. Like an anxious parent, a critic can only send it on its way and hope the world treats it kindly.

*Adventureland* is rated R and runs 107 minutes. For *Entertainment Weekly*’s take, click here.

**Review: “Adventureland” finds humor and heartbreak in a summer job from hell**

Greg Mottola’s **“Adventureland”** may arrive with the résumé of a broad teen comedy — it’s from the director of **“Superbad,”** after all — but the film is a quieter, more wistful piece of work. Set in the summer of 1987, it trades the frantic, raunchy momentum of Mottola’s earlier hit for something more reflective: a coming-of-age story about disappointment, first love, bad jobs and the slow realization that adulthood rarely shows up on schedule.

**Jesse Eisenberg** stars as James Brennan, a recent college graduate whose plans for a European trip and graduate school are derailed when his parents’ finances collapse. Forced to take a summer job at the run-down amusement park Adventureland, James enters the familiar purgatory of early adulthood: overeducated, underpaid and emotionally unprepared for the future.

Eisenberg plays James with his trademark nervous intelligence, but the performance is less ironic than vulnerable. He’s not simply the awkward guy in the room; he’s someone whose ideas about romance, class and maturity are constantly being tested. His fumbling sincerity gives the movie much of its emotional weight.

Opposite him, **Kristen Stewart** gives one of her most affecting early performances as Em, a co-worker whose guarded coolness masks a complicated inner life. Stewart’s restrained style fits the character beautifully. Em is neither a dream girl nor a stock love interest; she’s messy, conflicted and sometimes frustrating in ways that make her feel genuinely young. The chemistry between Eisenberg and Stewart is understated, built less on big romantic gestures than on shared cigarettes, late-night conversations and the awkward pauses that often say more than dialogue.

The **1980s setting** is more than a nostalgia machine, though the soundtrack — heavy with The Replacements, Lou Reed and other era-appropriate selections — does plenty of atmospheric work. Mottola uses the period to evoke a pre-digital kind of isolation, when bad decisions couldn’t be instantly explained away by a text message and summer jobs created temporary little worlds of their own. The amusement park, with its rigged games and faded attractions, becomes a fitting metaphor for young adulthood: bright lights on the surface, disappointment just underneath.

Compared with **“Superbad,” “Adventureland”** is less interested in comic escalation than emotional accumulation. Where “Superbad” turned adolescent panic into high-energy farce, “Adventureland” lingers on the aftermath of embarrassment, rejection and longing. There are laughs — especially from the park’s eccentric employees, including characters played by Bill Hader and Kristen Wiig — but the humor is gentler, more observational. Viewers expecting another nonstop barrage of outrageous set pieces may be surprised by how melancholy the film feels.

That melancholy is also its strength. “Adventureland” understands that coming of age is not a single breakthrough moment but a series of small humiliations and compromises. It captures the strange intensity of a summer that seems insignificant while it’s happening and formative only in retrospect.

Funny, tender and sharply acted, **“Adventureland”** stands as a more mature companion to “Superbad” — not as instantly quotable, perhaps, but richer in feeling. It’s a film about the jobs we take because we have no choice, the people we meet by accident and the versions of ourselves we leave behind when summer ends.

counterfactuals.output:
**Film Review: “Adventureland”**

**Rated:** R for language, drug use and sexual references  
**Runtime:** 107 minutes  
**Director:** Greg Mottola  
**Cast:** Jesse Eisenberg, Kristen Stewart, Ryan Reynolds, Martin Starr, Bill Hader, Kristen Wiig, Margarita Levieva  

Greg Mottola’s **“Adventureland”** arrives dressed like a teen comedy — a summer job, a shabby amusement park, awkward flirtations, pot smoke, cheap beer and humiliating uniforms — but its real ambitions are gentler and more melancholy. This is not a film about one wild summer so much as one disappointing summer that turns out, almost in spite of itself, to matter.

Set in 1987, the movie follows **James Brennan** (Jesse Eisenberg), a recent college graduate whose plans for a celebratory trip to Europe are abruptly canceled when his parents’ financial troubles force him to get a summer job. Overeducated, underexperienced and ill-prepared for manual labor, James finds himself working at **Adventureland**, a run-down amusement park in Pittsburgh where the games are rigged, the prizes are cheap and the employees are as lost as the customers.

There, James meets **Em Lewin** (Kristen Stewart), a co-worker with a dry wit, wounded confidence and more emotional baggage than she initially lets on. Their connection forms the center of the film: tentative, funny, messy and constantly threatened by misunderstandings, insecurity and the presence of **Mike Connell** (Ryan Reynolds), the park’s too-cool maintenance man who claims to have once jammed with Lou Reed and seems to have a troubling hold over Em.

Mottola, who previously directed **“Superbad,”** is working in a quieter register here. “Adventureland” has laughs, but it is not built as a joke machine. Its comedy comes from behavior: the absurdity of dead-end summer work, the forced cheer of customer service, the low-grade tyranny of supervisors, the way young adults try to sound worldly while making terrible decisions. The park itself is a terrific setting — bright lights over cracked pavement, pop songs blaring from speakers, carnival games designed to crush hope one ring toss at a time.

The supporting cast gives the film much of its comic texture. **Bill Hader and Kristen Wiig** play Bobby and Paulette, the husband-and-wife managers of Adventureland, with just the right blend of manic authority and small-time desperation. They are broadly funny without feeling imported from a sketch. **Martin Starr**, as James’ gloomy, pipe-smoking friend Joel, is another standout. His timing is beautifully dry, and he gives the film some of its best throwaway lines and most pointed observations about class, taste and disappointment.

Eisenberg is well cast as James, whose intelligence often exceeds his courage. He plays the character as nervous but not empty, privileged but not smug, idealistic but not naïve enough to be unbelievable. James can be frustrating, particularly in his self-absorption, but Eisenberg gives him a decency that keeps the character sympathetic.

Stewart, meanwhile, gives one of the film’s strongest performances. Em could easily have been reduced to a brooding “cool girl” with a secret pain, but Stewart makes her guardedness feel lived-in. She suggests a young woman who is perceptive enough to see the traps around her but not quite strong enough to avoid them. Her scenes with Eisenberg have a low-key emotional charge; their attraction feels less like movie destiny than the fragile recognition between two lonely people.

Ryan Reynolds is also effective in a deliberately deflated role. Connell is handsome, confident and vaguely glamorous in the eyes of the younger employees, but the film gradually reveals him as a man who has mistaken local celebrity for depth. Reynolds plays him with charm, but also with a faintly sour edge, allowing the audience to see why he is appealing and why he is pathetic.

What gives “Adventureland” its staying power is its attention to the indignities of early adulthood. The movie understands that being young is not always liberating; sometimes it is broke, confused, embarrassed and stuck in a job that smells like fried food. James believes he is on pause until his “real life” begins, but the film wisely recognizes that this, too, is real life.

The 1980s setting is used more for mood than nostalgia. The soundtrack — featuring The Replacements, Lou Reed, The Cure and other period-appropriate selections — does a great deal of atmospheric work, but Mottola avoids turning the decade into a costume party. The film’s pastness is present in the music, clothes and attitudes, yet its anxieties feel contemporary: money, sex, identity, family disappointment and the fear of becoming ordinary.

The humor is sharpest when it stays observational. Customers try to win impossible games; employees mock them while depending on their business; everyone at the park behaves as though the place is beneath them, even as it becomes the center of their social universe. Hader’s recurring warnings about not giving away the “giant-ass panda” are the sort of running gag that works because it is rooted in the petty economics of a failing amusement park.

If “Adventureland” has a weakness, it is that its dramatic turns can occasionally feel familiar. The romantic complications, especially those involving Connell, follow a recognizable coming-of-age pattern. But the film’s emotional honesty helps offset its conventional structure. Mottola is less interested in surprising us than in getting the tone right, and he does: wistful without being sugary, funny without being cruel, nostalgic without pretending the past was simpler than it was.

At its core, “Adventureland” is about disillusionment — not the grand, tragic kind, but the everyday sort that comes when young people realize adulthood will not arrive with instructions. It is also about class and money in subtle ways: James’ summer is shaped by his parents’ financial reversal, Em’s life is complicated by family grief and obligation, and nearly everyone at the park is improvising a version of dignity on low wages.

The result is a film that sneaks up on you. It may not deliver the nonstop hilarity suggested by its marketing, especially for viewers expecting another “Superbad,” but it offers something more durable: a compassionate portrait of youth at the moment it begins to curdle into adulthood.

**“Adventureland” is funny, rueful and perceptive — a coming-of-age comedy with a bruised romantic heart.**

**Rating: 3.5 out of 4 stars**

**(CNN-style lede)** — It looks, at first glance, like another summer-job comedy: a gangly college graduate, a run-down amusement park, bad uniforms, cheap prizes and the promise of awkward romance under neon lights. But Greg Mottola’s *Adventureland* is less interested in the noisy machinery of teen-movie hijinks than in the quiet ache of being young, broke, overeducated and emotionally unprepared for adulthood.

Set in 1987 and released in 2009, *Adventureland* occupies a curious space between nostalgia piece, coming-of-age drama and low-key comedy. Mottola, coming off the broader success of *Superbad*, might have been expected to deliver another raunchy youth farce. Instead, he makes something more wistful and bruised: a film about arrested momentum, where the summer after college becomes not a launchpad but a holding pattern.

Jesse Eisenberg plays James Brennan, whose plans for a European vacation and graduate school are derailed by his family’s financial troubles. Forced to take a job at Adventureland, a shabby Pittsburgh amusement park, James becomes the kind of protagonist Eisenberg has since made familiar: intelligent, verbal, anxious, self-conscious to the point of paralysis. But his performance here is less brittle than some of his later work. He gives James a believable softness — a young man who wants to be worldly but is still painfully naïve, particularly about love, class and his own sense of entitlement.

Kristen Stewart’s Em is the film’s emotional center, and her performance is one of its strongest assets. Stewart resists making Em a standard-issue “cool girl” fantasy, even though the story sometimes risks framing her that way through James’ infatuated gaze. She plays Em as guarded, dryly funny and wounded, someone whose intelligence is inseparable from her disappointment. Her silences matter as much as her dialogue; she suggests a person used to managing other people’s expectations while quietly lowering her own. The chemistry between Stewart and Eisenberg works because it feels tentative and uneven, not prepackaged. Their connection is full of pauses, half-confessions and misread signals — which is to say, it feels young.

Mottola’s direction is gentle but not shapeless. He has an eye for the dead-end poetry of mundane places: rain-slicked parking lots, break rooms, game booths, suburban basements, the strange melancholy of amusement parks after dark. Adventureland itself is not just a backdrop but a metaphor that never feels too forced. It is a place designed to manufacture fun, staffed by people who are often bored, lonely or quietly desperate. The park’s faded glamour mirrors the film’s view of late adolescence: thrilling in theory, disappointing in practice, but still capable of sudden beauty.

What distinguishes *Adventureland* from many teen comedies is its balance of humor and sensitivity. The film has broad comic elements — Bill Hader and Kristen Wiig provide eccentric adult supervision, and Martin Starr brings deadpan bitterness as James’ friend Joel — but the comedy rarely overwhelms the characters. Even the jokes tend to come from embarrassment, class anxiety, romantic confusion and workplace absurdity rather than pure punchline machinery. Mottola understands that for many young people, humiliation and longing are happening at the same time.

That balance is not perfect. Some supporting characters are thinly drawn, and Ryan Reynolds’ Mike Connell, the older maintenance man whose charm masks a deep sadness and irresponsibility, occasionally feels more like a narrative device than a fully realized figure. The film also leans into certain indie coming-of-age conventions: the carefully curated soundtrack, the moody romantic triangle, the sensitive male protagonist learning painful truths through a more complicated woman. Viewers less sympathetic to James may find the film too forgiving of his self-pity.

Still, *Adventureland* succeeds because it treats youthful confusion as something more than a setup for crude jokes or easy uplift. It remembers that a summer can feel endless when you are living through it and fleeting once it is gone. Mottola’s film is funny, but its humor is softened by regret; it is romantic, but not naïve about damage; it is nostalgic, but not blind to the sadness beneath the era’s pop songs and carnival lights.

In the end, *Adventureland* is less about having the best summer of your life than realizing life will not begin exactly when and how you planned. Its pleasures are modest, but so are its revelations — and that modesty is precisely what makes the film linger.

**Review: “Adventureland” finds bittersweet laughs beyond the midway**

Set amid the fading lights and rigged games of a Pittsburgh-area amusement park, **“Adventureland”** is less a raucous teen comedy than a wistful coming-of-age story disguised in carnival uniform. The film follows James Brennan (Jesse Eisenberg), a recent college graduate whose summer plans collapse, forcing him into a low-paying job at the local theme park in 1987.

Written and directed by **Greg Mottola**, best known to many moviegoers for directing the Judd Apatow-produced hit **“Superbad,”** “Adventureland” arrives with some comedy credentials — including Apatow-world associations through cast and tone — but it operates in a gentler, more melancholy register. The jokes are there, particularly in the awkward banter among underpaid park employees, but the film is more interested in disappointment, first love and the uneasy transition into adulthood.

Kristen Stewart plays Em, James’ co-worker and romantic interest, with a guarded sadness that gives the movie much of its emotional weight. **Ryan Reynolds** appears in a supporting role as Connell, the park’s too-cool maintenance man whose charm masks a less flattering reality. Reynolds brings charisma to the part, though the film is careful to complicate the character rather than simply use him as comic relief.

The **1987 soundtrack** is one of the movie’s strongest assets, steeped in songs from the Replacements, Lou Reed, Hüsker Dü and other era-defining acts. Rather than functioning as nostalgic decoration, the music helps establish the film’s mood: romantic, anxious and slightly bruised.

That mood may also be a commercial challenge. Audiences expecting another broad, gag-heavy comedy in the vein of “Superbad” could be surprised by how subdued “Adventureland” really is. Its carnival setting suggests wacky summer chaos, but the movie is more bittersweet than explosive, more observant than outrageous.

Still, for viewers willing to meet it on its own terms, “Adventureland” offers an affectionate, funny and quietly affecting look at a summer when nothing goes as planned — and everything feels important anyway.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a sophisticated review of the 2009 film “Adventureland,” focusing on its autobiographical basis, awkward young-adult romance, supporting cast, comparison to “Superbad,” and its mature treatment of immature characters.
counterfactuals.output:
Greg Mottola’s *Adventureland* (2009) arrived with the mild burden of expectation: it was the follow-up, at least in public perception, to *Superbad*, the riotous 2007 comedy he directed from Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg’s script. But where *Superbad* barrels forward on hormonal panic and escalating absurdity, *Adventureland* lingers. It is not a lesser teen comedy so much as a sly rebuke to the idea that coming-of-age stories must be powered by conquest, humiliation, or triumph. This is a film about the anticlimax of youth: the summer that feels like a detour while you’re living it, and like an origin story years later.

The film’s autobiographical basis is central to its texture. Mottola wrote and directed *Adventureland* from memories of working at an amusement park in the 1980s, and the movie has the specificity of lived experience rather than the broadness of nostalgic reconstruction. The titular park is not presented as a magical liminal space where misfits blossom under neon lights; it is sticky, cheap, repetitive, faintly depressing. The games are rigged, the prizes are pathetic, the rides seem held together by paint and inertia. That drabness is one of the movie’s greatest strengths. Mottola understands that many formative experiences are not obviously cinematic while they’re happening. They become meaningful because of the people who happen to be there, the mistakes made in boredom, and the private humiliations that hindsight eventually softens.

Jesse Eisenberg plays James Brennan, a recent college graduate whose plans for a European summer and graduate school are derailed by his parents’ financial troubles. Forced to take a job at Adventureland, James arrives with the wounded entitlement of an overeducated young man discovering that the world is indifferent to his self-image. Eisenberg is perfectly cast: his nervous intelligence, verbal hesitation, and flickers of moral vanity make James both sympathetic and quietly exasperating. He is not a geek hero in the wish-fulfillment sense. He is often kind, but he is also self-absorbed; romantic, but prone to idealization; insecure, but not without an ego. The film’s maturity lies partly in refusing to mistake sensitivity for virtue.

The romance between James and Em Lewin, played by Kristen Stewart, is one of the most observant depictions of awkward young-adult attraction in American comedy of its era. Their connection is built from half-finished conversations, cigarette breaks, shared music, and glances that carry more weight than declarations. Stewart’s performance is unusually guarded and bruised, especially compared with the more schematic “dream girl” roles often assigned to young women in male coming-of-age stories. Em is neither a prize nor a puzzle to be solved. She is a young woman making bad decisions out of grief, loneliness, and a low estimation of what she deserves. Her relationship with Ryan Reynolds’s Connell, the park’s married maintenance man and resident local legend, is treated not as a melodramatic betrayal but as a sad, plausible entanglement. The emotional stakes are small on paper and enormous in the moment, which is precisely the register the movie understands best.

That delicacy is what most separates *Adventureland* from *Superbad*. The comparison is inevitable, but not especially illuminating if limited to genre. Both films involve young men confronting sex, friendship, and the terror of moving on, yet their rhythms are almost opposite. *Superbad* is a last-night-of-high-school farce, structured around momentum and comic catastrophe. *Adventureland* is a summer-after-college memory piece, structured around drift and accumulation. Its comedy is quieter, more situational, often tinged with embarrassment rather than punchline release. If *Superbad* captures the frantic vulgarity of adolescence at the point of rupture, *Adventureland* captures the melancholy just after, when freedom has technically arrived but adulthood remains humiliatingly out of reach.

The supporting cast gives the film much of its lived-in charm. Martin Starr, as Joel, provides a wonderfully dry portrait of intellectual disappointment, hiding deep feeling beneath deadpan resignation. His friendship with James is one of the film’s understated pleasures, especially because it is allowed to be prickly and imperfect. Bill Hader and Kristen Wiig, as the park’s managers, could have wandered in from a broader comedy, but they calibrate their absurdity carefully; they are ridiculous without puncturing the film’s atmosphere. Their recurring announcements and managerial rituals evoke the strange theater of low-wage work, where petty authority becomes its own form of performance. Ryan Reynolds, meanwhile, uses his charm in a more unsettling key. Connell is not a cartoon villain, but a man who has learned to coast on charisma, myth, and other people’s willingness to believe in him. Even the minor figures—the park workers, local toughs, and bored customers—help create a world that feels socially cramped and emotionally revealing.

Mottola’s handling of the 1980s setting is also refreshingly restrained. The period details—music, clothes, cars, Lou Reed, Hüsker Dü, Falco’s “Rock Me Amadeus” blaring with comic insistence—are vivid but not embalmed in nostalgia. The soundtrack in particular functions less as a greatest-hits compilation than as emotional geography. These are songs people use to define themselves, impress one another, or survive a shift. The film understands the way taste can become a romantic language when you are young, especially when you don’t yet know how to say what you mean directly.

What makes *Adventureland* endure is its mature treatment of immature characters. Its people lie, sulk, posture, drink too much, confuse desire with destiny, and hurt one another in banal, recognizable ways. But the film does not sneer at them. Nor does it excuse them entirely. Mottola’s perspective is affectionate but unsentimental: youth is funny because it is so dramatic, and painful because the drama is real to the person living it. James and Em are not transformed by love into better, clearer versions of themselves. They simply move, haltingly, toward honesty. That is a modest arc, but an emotionally credible one.

In the end, *Adventureland* is less about an amusement park than about the gap between expectation and experience. James expects Europe and gets a game booth; he expects romance and gets confusion; he expects adulthood to begin with purpose and instead finds it beginning with minimum wage, jealousy, and cheap corn dogs. The film’s wisdom is that this disappointment is not incidental to growing up—it is growing up. Funny, rueful, and beautifully acted, *Adventureland* is a comedy of delayed arrival, one that recognizes how often our most important summers feel, at the time, like accidents.
